transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-19
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 47 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Hightide Head of ML), Marco Rivera (Eng Lead), Jenna Park (Infra), Samir Desai (Product)

Summary:
- Customer is evaluating porting serving from Anthropic/OpenAI + in-house vLLM/TGI stack into a consolidated solution. They are weighing Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private Redwood offerings. Primary concerns: parity on output (eval), latency targets for production chat, cost per 1M tokens, and security/KMS integration for PII workloads.

Topics Covered:
- Current stack and pain points (vLLM/TGI reliability, ops overhead)
- Eval parity strategy and regression testing
- Dedicated capacity sizing and autoscale for peak holiday loads
- Private (VPC) deployment, KMS/HSM, and audit logs
- Quantization and performance tradeoffs
- Next steps: pilot, security docs, benchmark run

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Okay folks thanks for joining, uh I think we have like 45, 50 minutes blocked? I see Priya, Marco, Jenna, Samir. Hi everyone. Quick intros on our side, I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, Liam's our SE and will do the deeper parts.
[00:18] Priya Kapoor: Hi yeah I'm Priya, head of ML at Hightide. We own the models and the inference stack, currently running a mix of Anthropic for safety-sensitive flows and some OpenAI for assistant generation, but router goes to vLLM + TGI on-prem for lower-cost bulk inference.
[00:33] Marco Rivera: Marco here, engineering lead on serving. We're trying to reduce ops overhead and also get more predictable latency during sales events, and also cut inference cost without regressing quality.
[00:44] Liam O'Connor: Great, thanks. Can you say briefly what your current p95/p99 look like and what latency SLO you need?
[00:52] Priya Kapoor: Sure. Right now p95 is around 220 to 300 ms for short chat prompts on vLLM infra, p99 spikes to 700ms under load. Our target is p95 < 200ms and p99 < 400ms for the interactive assistant. Cost-wise we expect to be within 60% of current spend or better.
[01:15] Maya Chen: Got it. And are you mixing hosted Anthropic/OpenAI for some calls and routing others to your infra—so there's an extra routing layer?
[01:24] Marco Rivera: Yeah we have a router that sends safety-sensitive prompts to Anthropic and high-throughput batch requests through TGI/vLLM on our cluster. The router logic is getting hairy.
[01:33] Samir Desai: Also the compliance team wants archive audit logs and customer-level retention for up to 3 years for some enterprise accounts.
[01:41] Maya Chen: Ok good, that's exactly the sort of constraints we've helped other retailers with. Quick high-level: Redwood can offer Hosted for fastest migration, Dedicated for predictable capacity (SLA), and Private (VPC / on-prem) if you need full network isolation and customer-managed KMS.
[01:58] Priya Kapoor: So, two things: 1) We need eval parity — outputs must match within our quality thresholds compared to Anthropic/OpenAI. 2) We need deterministic latency under holiday spikes. How do you do eval parity without retraining?
[02:14] Liam O'Connor: Good question. We do model variant mapping and run parital evals — sorry partial — we map your current model flavors to the closest version we host, then run your prompt suite through both stacks and generate regression reports. We also support model-agnostic rerankers and safety hooks so you can keep the same safety pipeline.
[02:32] Marco Rivera: When you say "map to closest version" do you support TGI/vLLM-format models directly or do we need to convert weights? We use some community quantized checkpoints and custom kernels.
[02:43] Liam O'Connor: We support a wide matrix — we can host standard HF-compatible checkpoints as-is. For vLLM/TGI custom kernels, usually we need a compatibility step: either we run your binary on our Dedicated nodes for an initial test, or we guide a conversion to a Redwood-compatible variant. Occasionally the tokenizer differences or custom ops need a small patch. We've seen that about 10-15% of customer models need a tiny glue change.
[03:04] Priya Kapoor: That aligns with our experience. What's your approach to KV cache and prefix caching? Our latency needs to be low for continuation tokens.
[03:15] Liam O'Connor: We have automatic KV cache handling in the runtime—by default we keep session KV cached with eviction policies. Prefix caching is supported for repeated system prompts. For your chat use-case we'd recommend warm KV + a small continuous-batching window to keep per-token latency down. There are tradeoffs vs. throughput.
[03:34] Jenna Park: Are caches encrypted? From a security perspective anything persisted needs to be encrypted at rest and we want KMS rotation.
[03:40] Maya Chen: Yes, on Private and Dedicated we support customer KMS integration; caches on disk can be encrypted and keys managed by customer KMS/HSM. For Hosted we offer Redwood-managed KMS with customer key wrap on enterprise plans.
[03:56] Marco Rivera: Also curious about quantization — currently we run int8/4 quantized checkpoints in vLLM. How much quality drop do you see if we switch to your quantized runtime?
[04:07] Liam O'Connor: It depends heavily on model family and prompt distribution. We have recommended quantization profiles — a lot of customers use int8 for general generation with negligible visible regression on chat, int4 for stable batch workloads. For eval parity we run blind A/B on your prompt set so you can measure regression rates. We'll include recommended deltas in the pilot config.
[04:25] Priya Kapoor: Cost math: do you have an example showing tokens per second, cost per million tokens on Dedicated vs Hosted?
[04:32] Maya Chen: We will send a cost sheet in the follow-up. Roughly, Dedicated committed capacity can cut per-token unit by 30-50% depending on utilization; Hosted is easiest to start with but can be 10-20% higher at scale. We'll include sample run numbers for your estimated QPS and sequence lengths.
[04:51] Samir Desai: One of our legal asks is SSO + SCIM provisioning and audit logs, can you do SAML and granular RBAC?
[04:58] Maya Chen: Yes, enterprise plans include SAML SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and long-term audit log retention as an add-on. We'll attach the security appendix.
[05:07] [00:05:07] Marco Rivera: On the ops side we want to understand failure modes: if a GPU node goes down during holiday peak, what happens to in-flight sessions and retries?
[05:17] Liam O'Connor: Our serving runtime supports request-level retries and automatic fallback to compatible model variants in a different capacity pool. For Dedicated, the autoscaler and buffer pools kick in; for Private you can configure warm standby nodes. We also provide tracing hooks so you can see exactly where retries occur.
[05:34] Priya Kapoor: Is there any vendor lock-in with Redwood's model formats? We have tooling built around vLLM's caching formats.
[05:41] Maya Chen: We focus on model portability; customers can always export served model artifacts and there are no proprietary weight encodings. There are runtime optimizations (kernels) that make us faster, but models remain HF-compatible.
[05:53] [00:05:53] Marco Rivera: Let's talk about pilot scope — we want to validate: 1) output parity for 5k prompts, 2) p95 latency under our traffic shape, 3) cost target within 60% of current. How long to set up a pilot?
[06:08] Liam O'Connor: Typical pilot is 2 weeks for a focused eval: week one for onboarding, converting any weights, running offline evals; week two for live traffic testing and scaling. If you require Private deployment, the install window can extend depending on network approvals, usually 2-4 weeks.
[06:23] Jenna Park: For the Private install, what's required from our infra team? VPC peering? Bastion?
[06:29] Maya Chen: For Private we need VPC peering, a small set of ports, and a service account for KMS integration. We can provide a one-page install checklist. For air-gapped installs there is a different package and timeline.
[06:41] Priya Kapoor: Can you run our same safety/rerank pipeline? We do a multi-stage safety check that uses an internal reranker after generation.
[06:49] Liam O'Connor: Absolutely. We can either run your reranker as a post-processing hook in the same request path or expose streaming responses and let your reranker consume them. Both patterns are supported; we can discuss performance implications.
[07:02] Samir Desai: Any mention of real-world customers in retail who migrated and saw cost or latency improvements?
[07:08] Maya Chen: We have a case with a commerce customer who consolidated from multi-vendor routing and saw p95 drop from ~300 ms to ~160 ms and reduced unit cost by ~40% after moving to Dedicated. We'll share anonymized numbers.
[07:20] [00:07:20] Marco Rivera: Ok, technical: what runtime versions do you support — do you expose the same APIs we're using with TGI? It matters for our orchestration glue.
[07:31] Liam O'Connor: We present a simple REST and streaming API. We also have a compatibility shim for TGI-style websocket streaming in our Dedicated and Private products; it maps tokens and events so minimal code changes are required on your side. The webhook/stream semantics are close, but not byte-for-byte identical.
[07:49] Priya Kapoor: About regression testing, do you provide tooling to run A/B blind evaluations? We need the statistical significance tests.
[07:56] Liam O'Connor: Yes, Redwood Optimize includes eval harnesses and we can run blind A/B tests with metrics (BLEU-like, ROUGE, and custom accuracy checks), and produce a regression report including statistically significant deltas. For customer pilots we typically include that as part of the deliverable.
[08:12] Priya Kapoor: One more thing — we use per-customer data retention and have PII redaction obligations. Can you configure retention per-route?
[08:20] Maya Chen: Yes, route-level retention and redaction policies are supported in Dedicated and Private. Hosted supports retention controls and can be configured to not persist prompts, but enterprise retention tiers may be required for per-customer long-term logs.
[08:36] Marco Rivera: Are you able to replicate our exact tokenizer behavior? We have custom pre-tokenization step for SKU parsing.
[08:44] Liam O'Connor: We can ingest a tokenizer artifact and run it in the runtime; if there's a custom preprocessing step we can either run it as a pre-hook on the router or you can pre-tokenize and send token ids. We've done that for other customers with SKU-aware tokenizers.
[08:58] [00:08:58] Samir Desai: Budget question: if we do Dedicated with a 12-month commit what does pricing look like compared to hosted?
[09:06] Maya Chen: We'll send a proposal. Typical committed Dedicated discounts range from 30-50% vs list hosted unit price depending on utilization and GPU class. We can model an example with your QPS, avg seq len, and concurrency.
[09:18] Priya Kapoor: I want to flag one risk — training drift: our models update frequently. How does Redwood handle frequent model rollouts and versioning without disrupting traffic?
[09:28] Liam O'Connor: Our rollout system supports canary, A/B, and automatic fallback. You can pin traffic percentages by model version and have safety gates based on eval sets. Rollbacks are instantaneous to the previous pinned version.
[09:37] Marco Rivera: Good. Can you give a sense of the quantization lift in throughput? If we move from fp16 to int8 on Dedicated, how much extra throughput?
[09:45] Liam O'Connor: On typical LLMs, int8 can give 1.3-1.8x throughput improvements depending on kernel support. For int4 it can be higher but at more risk to quality. We'll produce a profiling run during the pilot to show exact numbers.
[09:58] [00:09:58] Priya Kapoor: Real quick — how do you handle throttling and rate limits? We need graceful degradation rather than 5xxs for our storefront assistant under peak.
[10:06] Maya Chen: Redwood supports priority queues, backpressure, and graceful degradation policies. We can set fallbacks to smaller model variants, or queue requests and return provisional responses. Those are configurable per-route.
[10:18] Marco Rivera: If we wanted to run a small POC, say 30k interactions over two weeks, and keep traffic shape approximating Black Friday, what do you need from us to get started?
[10:26] Liam O'Connor: We'll need the eval prompt set (5k minimum), a short traffic simulation profile (QPS, distribution of seq lengths), access to a representative model checkpoint if you want exact parity testing, and network info for Private if relevant.
[10:40] Priya Kapoor: For the eval prompt set do you need labels or gold responses? We have both but some prompts are open-ended.
[10:48] Liam O'Connor: Labels are helpful for objective metrics; for subjective generation we run human evals or use your internal rubric. We'll combine automated metrics and sample human reviews.
[10:59] [00:10:59] Jenna Park: Security — can we run a tabletop incident response drill with Redwood? Our SOC team likes to exercise chain-of-custody.
[11:06] Maya Chen: Yes, we can do a short tabletop and include the incident response playbook as part of the security docs.
[11:12] Priya Kapoor: Any limitations with private data inside prompts — do you allow running on encrypted memory?
[11:19] Liam O'Connor: We support memory encryption at rest and in some Private deployments we can enable confidential compute features where available. For middleware redaction we recommended client-side pre-redaction for PII.
[11:30] [00:11:30] Maya Chen: Great. To recap, sounds like next steps: Maya will share security appendix, SOC2, KMS integration notes, and pricing/pilot template. Liam will sketch out recommended Dedicated sizing and quantization profiles. Hightide will share prompt set, traffic profile, and infra diagram. Any blockers?
[11:48] Priya Kapoor: Timing — we'd like pilot to start late May if Private installs don't block us. If Private takes too long we may start with Hosted or Dedicated.
[11:58] Maya Chen: That works. We'll aim to have the follow-up package by 2026-05-21 so you can sign off on the pilot quickly.
[12:05] Samir Desai: One last thing, who will be our Redwood point of contact for the pilot day-to-day?
[12:11] Maya Chen: I'll be overall AE owner; Liam will be SE lead. Noah may join for ops setup. We'll include Slack channel invite in the follow-up.
[12:22] [00:12:22] Marco Rivera: Cool. Thanks everyone, this was useful.
[12:26] Maya Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the doc bundle.
[12:30] End of call.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-hear of vLLM as 'V-L-L-M' and TGI as 'T-G-I' spelled out; some proper nouns (SKU names) redacted/mis-transcribed.
